title: Psalm 108: An Old Song Sung Again
summary: The psalmist wakes the dawn with music and praises God among the nations for a love higher than the heavens. He then recalls an old oracle in which God claims the land of Israel and its hostile neighbors as his own, and asks who will lead the army into Edom. The psalm ends with a confession that human help is worthless and a confident hope that God will win the battle.
story: Psalm 108 opens a small group of three psalms of David (108 to 110) near the start of Book V, the last of the five collections that make up the Psalter. Book V begins with Psalm 107, which gives thanks for people gathered back from the lands where they had been scattered. The returned community still lived under foreign rule and still faced old enemies, and Psalm 108 puts David's own words back into their mouths. It is made almost entirely of two earlier psalms: verses 1 to 5 repeat Psalm 57:7-11, and verses 6 to 13 repeat Psalm 60:5-12. A song of confident praise is joined to a prayer for victory after defeat, and the combination reads as a people who have been rejected and restored asking God to finish what he promised.
historical:
The heading calls the psalm “A song. A Psalm of David.” Its two source psalms carry their own headings in the Psalter: Psalm 57 is linked with David's flight from Saul into a cave, and Psalm 60 with his wars against the Arameans and the Edomites (compare 2 Samuel 8). Psalm 108 drops those settings, which suggests that someone deliberately rearranged older Davidic material for a new use. When that happened is not known. Many scholars think the combination was made after the exile, when the editors of the Psalter were shaping Book V; others think it could have been made during the monarchy for a particular military crisis. The superscriptions are ancient; many scholars think editors added them, while others regard them as reliable early tradition, and interpreters differ on how much historical weight to give them. The phrase “of David” can mean written by David, belonging to a Davidic collection, or written in his manner.

The focus on Edom would have carried a sharp edge after 587 or 586 BC. Edom, Judah's neighbor to the southeast, took advantage of Jerusalem's fall to Babylon, and later texts such as Obadiah and Psalm 137:7 remember that betrayal bitterly. A reader in the Persian period would hear the question “Who will lead me to Edom?” with that memory in mind.
cultural:
Ordinarily the dawn wakes the sleeper, and the psalmist reverses the image: instead of the dawn waking him, he will wake the dawn with harp and lyre. These were the two standard stringed instruments of Israel's worship. The oracle in verses 7 to 9 then walks around the map. Shechem lay in the central hill country west of the Jordan, and the Valley of Succoth lay east of the river; Gilead and part of Manasseh were east of the Jordan too. God claims both banks. Ephraim, the strongest northern tribe, is his helmet, and Judah, the royal tribe, is his scepter, echoing Jacob's blessing that the scepter would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10).

The neighbors receive humbler roles. Moab becomes a washbasin, a menial household vessel. Throwing a sandal over Edom has been read in two ways: as a gesture of contempt, or as a legal act of taking possession, since a sandal figures in a property transfer in Ruth 4:7. Either way, the enemy nations are pictured as pieces of the divine warrior's household. The fortified city in verse 10 is probably an Edomite stronghold in the rugged hills south of the Dead Sea.
literary: The psalm is a composite. The first half is a hymn of praise with a vow to sing among the nations; the second is a communal prayer that quotes a divine oracle (verses 7 to 9) and then asks in plain distress whether God has rejected his people. Joined together, the order is reversed from what a reader might expect: confident praise comes first, and the complaint follows. The effect is that the complaint is framed by trust. The poem uses parallel lines throughout, and it moves from singular (“My heart is steadfast”) to plural (“save us”) and back, so that one voice speaks for the whole people. The closing verse turns the question of verse 11 into an answer: God will march out after all.

outline.t: A steadfast heart wakes the dawn
Praise among the nations for love beyond the heavens
God's oracle: the land and the nations are his
Who will lead us? Has God rejected us?
Human help fails; with God we will prevail

doctrines.note: The oracle claims every territory, Israelite and foreign, as God's possession. Victory is not the army's achievement but God's decision, which is why the psalm can say plainly that “the help of man is worthless.”
The psalm shows Israel praying with old words. Faith here is not inventing new speech but taking up promises already given and asking God to keep them in a new situation.
The psalmist vows to praise God “among the nations” and prays that his glory will cover the earth. Even a psalm about war with neighbors has the whole world in view as the audience of God's praise.

words.note: Chesed, rendered “loving devotion” in the BSB. It is God's loyal, covenant love, the kindness he binds himself to show. Here it extends “beyond the heavens,” a picture of love larger than the created world. It is the ground for asking God to act in verse 6.

Kun, to be established or firm. “My heart is steadfast” describes a heart settled and fixed, not wavering. The psalm begins with this settled heart before it names any crisis, so trust is the starting point rather than the reward for victory.

Kavod, glory, from a root meaning weight. In verse 1 the Hebrew says that the psalmist will sing with his glory as well, which the BSB renders “with all my being,” meaning the honor and substance of the self. In verse 5 the same word is God's glory covering the earth. The same word links the worshiper's own honor, offered in song, to God's glory over all the earth.

Zanach, to reject or cast off. The word is strong and personal, used for spurning something. The psalm does not hide the experience of feeling abandoned by God; it states it as a question and brings it straight to him.

christ: The New Testament does not quote Psalm 108, so the connection is thematic rather than predictive. The psalm voices the hope that a son of David would lead God's people to victory and that God's praise would be sung among the nations. The Gospels present Jesus as that son of David, but his victory comes by a different road: he wins not by marching into Edom but by the cross and resurrection, and his people then carry his praise to every nation (Matthew 28:18-20). Paul gathers several psalm texts about the nations praising God (Romans 15:9-11) to show that the gospel for Gentiles was always Israel's hope, and verse 3 of this psalm belongs to the same stream.

hard.q: Why would the Psalter repeat parts of two earlier psalms, and does that make this psalm less inspired?
hard.a: Repetition is not unusual in Scripture. Psalm 14 and Psalm 53 are nearly identical, and Psalm 18 appears also in 2 Samuel 22. Ancient Israel treated its songs as living material that could be reused and reshaped for new needs, much as churches today set old hymns to new tunes or combine texts for a service. On this reading, Psalm 108 is a deliberate new composition: an editor chose the most confident lines of Psalm 57 and the most urgent lines of Psalm 60 and set them side by side for a new generation. Readers who hold a high view of Scripture's inspiration generally see the Spirit at work in the editing as well as in the first writing, and the final form of the Psalter is the form the church received. Critical scholars ask more about when and why the combination was made; either way, the psalm teaches that God's earlier promises can be prayed again.

questions: The psalm puts praise before the complaint. What would change in your own prayers if you began with what you know of God's love before you named what is wrong?
Verse 12 says that human help is worthless. Where are you most tempted to trust in human help, and what would it look like to trust God there without being passive?
The psalm reuses older words for a new crisis. Which passages of Scripture have you returned to in different seasons, and how did they speak differently each time?
